claims.statement: People weigh suffering more than happiness when judging whether a population is net positive: on average 1.5-3 times as many happy as unhappy people are required, and the asymmetry persists (smaller) when the two experiences are stipulated to be equally intense (Studies 1a-1c).
claims.scope: US MTurk adults (Positly), 2019-2020; single free-response percentage item 'what % happy vs unhappy for this world to be overall positive (better to exist than not)'; Study 1a extreme intensities (N=474), 1b 2x2 intensities with a -100..+100 scale (N=356), 1c mild and stipulated-equal intensities (N=278).

quantities.baseline: Study 1a, extreme happiness ('falling in love') vs extreme suffering ('torture'), pooled inter- and intra-individual conditions; 50 = symmetric weighting

quantities.name: happiness_share_required_for_net_positive_population
quantities.baseline: Study 1c, mild intensities STIPULATED equal and accepted by the participant; pooled conditions

quantities.name: happiness_per_unhappiness_trade_ratio_median
quantities.unit: happy people per unhappy person (individual h/(100-h), median)
quantities.source: reanalysis/s1.py; responses of exactly 100 (n=24) have an infinite ratio and are excluded from the ratio but not from the median's ordering
quantities.baseline: Study 1a pooled; ratio of means 3.05, geometric mean 3.66, arithmetic mean of individual ratios 9.19 -- the paper's '3 times' is the median and the ratio-of-means, not the mean person

quantities.unit: happy people per unhappy person (individual, median)
quantities.baseline: Study 1c pooled (stipulated equal intensity)

quantities.name: share_symmetric_weighting_50_or_51
quantities.baseline: Study 1c; modal response is 51 (n=67)

quantities.name: share_symmetric_weighting_50_or_51
quantities.baseline: Study 1a (extreme intensities)

quantities.name: share_requiring_100pct_happiness
quantities.baseline: Study 1a: no amount of happiness offsets any torture-level suffering (strict-negative-utilitarian-like answer)

quantities.name: share_weighting_happiness_more_than_suffering
quantities.baseline: Study 1a, responses < 50

our_assessment.why: Every N, exclusion count, mean, SD and t reproduces from the deposit. The 'average person' framing is the soft part: in 1c the answers are a two-cluster mixture -- 37% at 50/51 (symmetric) and a spread of asymmetric weighters -- and the mean (61) is a value few people gave. The centre is honestly reported (the paper mentions the mode of 51); the decomposition is what a reader citing '1.5x' should carry. Individual trade ratios are heavy-tailed (1a: median 3.0, arithmetic mean 9.2), so 'people require 3x' is a median statement.

claims.statement: In Study 1b (2 happiness intensity x 2 suffering intensity), intensity of suffering and of happiness both matter, with no significant interaction (F(1,352)=2.85, p=.09): the required share of happy people rises when suffering is extreme and when happiness is mild.
claims.scope: Study 1b, N=356, between-subjects, ANOVA on the raw percentage.

quantities.name: intensity_interaction_on_logit_happiness_share
quantities.unit: log-odds (HC3 OLS interaction mild-happiness x extreme-suffering)
quantities.ci: SE 0.346, p=0.0048; clipping 0.1-2.0 points gives 0.76-1.11, p=0.004-0.011; excluding 0/100 answers 0.70, p=0.030
quantities.baseline: logit of the stated % happy, i.e. log of the implied trade ratio -- the scale on which the paper itself interprets the result ('1.5-3 times')

quantities.name: intensity_interaction_on_percentage_scale
quantities.baseline: raw percentage, authors' ANOVA

quantities.name: median_trade_ratio_mild_happiness_vs_extreme_suffering
quantities.baseline: 1b cell; the other three cells: extreme/extreme 3.0, extreme-happy/mild-suffering 1.86, mild/mild 1.5

our_assessment.why: The 'no interaction' is a property of the percentage scale. On the log-ratio scale -- the one the paper uses to state its conclusion -- the interaction is positive and significant across every clipping choice and in a median-based bootstrap (1.31, 95% CI 0.30-1.79). Read on that scale: the intensity of HAPPINESS barely matters when suffering is mild (log-odds +0.05) and matters a great deal when suffering is extreme. A known-answer simulation (no true log-scale interaction, cell effects matched to the data) gives a 5.2% rejection rate for the logit test and 5.4% for the percentage test, so the logit result is not a transformation artifact; with a true interaction of 0.7 the percentage ANOVA has 72% power and the logit test 91%. Which scale is 'right' is not decidable from the data (an interaction without crossover is removable by a monotone transform); the paper simply did not say which scale its null was on.

claims.statement: People do not regard creating new people as neutral: adding an extremely happy person makes a world better and adding an extremely unhappy person makes it worse, symmetrically (no procreation asymmetry), and there is a weak general preference to add even a neutral person (Studies 2a-2b).
claims.scope: 2a: within-subjects, N=157, world of 1 million neutral people (the paper's Study 2b section says '10 million' -- the materials say 1 million). 2b: between-subjects 2x2 (empty vs 10 billion; happy vs unhappy), Prolific, N=369. 7-point scale.

quantities.name: share_full_neutrality_about_creating_people
quantities.baseline: Study 2a: rated BOTH the +100 and the -100 addition as 'equally good' (4)

quantities.name: share_procreation_asymmetry_mcmahan
quantities.baseline: Study 2a: unhappy addition worse, happy addition exactly neutral

quantities.name: share_reverse_procreation_asymmetry
quantities.baseline: Study 2a: happy addition better, unhappy addition exactly neutral -- the mirror of McMahan

quantities.name: share_both_additions_count
quantities.baseline: Study 2a: happy better AND unhappy worse; among these the magnitude asymmetry is exactly 0.00 (Wilcoxon p=0.99)

quantities.name: share_wrong_sign_responders
quantities.baseline: Study 2a: rated adding a -100 life as an improvement (15) or a +100 life as a worsening (6); 3 did both

quantities.name: neutral_person_addition_preference_d
quantities.baseline: Study 2a EXCLUDING the 18 wrong-sign responders (paper, all 157: d=0.35). The 11.5% wrong-sign group supplies 51.4% of the total excess above 4.

quantities.name: neutral_person_addition_mean_full_world
quantities.baseline: Study 2b, world of 10 billion, consistent responders; empty world 4.246, p<0.0001

our_assessment.why: The symmetry survives at the level of individual types, which is a stronger result than the paper reports: the McMahan asymmetry (7.6%) is matched by its own mirror image (6.4%), and among people who count both additions the magnitudes are identical. Two qualifications. (1) 'People reject the intuition of neutrality' is a majority statement: 12% hold full neutrality and another 7.6% are neutral about the happy addition -- about one in five are neutral about creating a maximally happy person. (2) The 'weak general preference to add a neutral person' is half carried by the 11.5% who also answered in the wrong direction on the main items, and in 2b it exists only for the EMPTY world (4.25) and not for a world of 10 billion (4.02, p=0.21): it is a preference for there being someone, not for there being more people.

claims.statement: Asymmetric scope sensitivity (Study 3a): people prefer larger happy and smaller unhappy populations, the preference for smaller unhappy populations is stronger, and the asymmetry GROWS with absolute size -- preference for larger happy populations declines and even reverses at 1 billion vs 10 billion, while preference for smaller unhappy populations persists.
claims.scope: Study 3a, N=789 (402 happy arm, 387 unhappy arm), three 10x comparisons (1k/10k, 1M/10M, 1B/10B), 7-point preference; each participant then answered the SAME three comparisons for neutral populations.

quantities.name: size_trend_asymmetry_raw
quantities.unit: difference between arms in (1k-minus-1b) raw preference, 7-pt scale
quantities.source: reanalysis/s3a.py (reproduces the paper's t(773)=5.05 to rounding; the paper's df differs)
quantities.baseline: authors' test of 'asymmetry grows with size'

quantities.name: size_trend_asymmetry_neutral_differenced
quantities.unit: same, after subtracting each participant's own neutral answer at the same size
quantities.baseline: using the neutral items as a per-size baseline, as the paper's own covariate logic does in aggregate

quantities.name: neutral_item_size_trend_difference_between_arms
quantities.unit: 7-pt scale; identical neutral items, happy arm 1.483 vs unhappy arm 0.840
quantities.baseline: the neutral items are identical in both arms and asked after the main task; any difference is carry-over (or chance)

quantities.name: share_identical_answers_happy_and_neutral_populations
quantities.baseline: happy arm: same answer for happy and neutral populations at all three sizes (unhappy arm: 83/387 = 0.214)

quantities.name: welfare_attributable_preference_for_larger_happy_population
quantities.unit: 7-pt scale, happy minus own neutral answer
quantities.baseline: 1B vs 10B; the raw answer (3.71) is BELOW 4 -- the 'reversal' -- while the differenced answer is positive at every size (0.45, 0.50, 0.53)

our_assessment.why: Reverse-coding the unhappy arm turns any valence-neutral preference for SMALLER populations (crowding, which the paper's own participants mention) into an apparent valence asymmetry that grows with size. Built two worlds that give the identical six cell means -- one with perfectly SYMMETRIC welfare scope sensitivity plus a common size aversion rising from -0.08 to 0.98 scale points, one with asymmetric welfare and no size aversion -- and the authors' test rejects in 98% and 99.7% of simulated studies in both (reanalysis/s3a_identifiability.py). The neutral items that could separate the worlds are post-treatment: identical across arms, yet their size trend differs by arm (p=2e-6) and 35% of the happy arm copied their answers verbatim. They therefore cannot be used as a baseline -- neither for my per-size differencing (under which the growing asymmetry and the 1B reversal vanish completely) nor for the authors' size-averaged covariate. What the data DO support: a LEVEL asymmetry (unhappy effect ~3x the happy effect at every size, in raw and in differenced scores alike), and a size aversion that both arms' neutral answers show (below 4 at 1B in both arms, whichever way carry-over pushed). What they cannot support: that sensitivity to the number of happy people specifically decays with scale. The fix is cheap and future-facing: a separately randomised neutral arm.

claims.statement: When average and total conflict, people apply both principles, with a threshold for minimally acceptable average: 1000 people at +100 is roughly as good as 100,000 at +70, but even 1 billion at +50 does not outweigh 1000 at +100; reflection shifts answers toward totalism (Study 3c, N=461; Study 3d mere addition, N=482; Study 3b equal totals, N=825).
claims.scope: Studies 3b-3d, MTurk, 7-point preference between two specified civilisations on a -100..+100 scale; 3c excluded 159/622 (26%) for failing 'how does someone at level 0 feel' (96 of them said 'extremely unhappy').

quantities.baseline: Study 3c happy populations, intuition condition; reflection 0.298 (0.00-0.60, n=101)

quantities.name: fraction_of_average_loss_recovered_by_10000x_population
quantities.baseline: Study 3c UNHAPPY populations, reflection condition; intuition 1.58 (0.91-4.44, n=128). Confounded with size aversion exactly as c4 is.

quantities.name: marginal_preference_per_log10_population_happy_beyond_1m
quantities.unit: 7-pt scale per factor of 10 (million@50 -> billion@50, 3 orders)
quantities.baseline: happy populations at +50; the first order of magnitude (100k -> 1M) moves 0.15-0.21

quantities.name: averagist_preference_equal_totals
quantities.unit: 7-pt (1 = smaller population with higher average, 4 = indifferent)
quantities.baseline: Study 3b, totals equal by construction

quantities.name: averagist_preference_equal_totals
quantities.baseline: Study 3b, ONLY the 46 of 825 (5.6%) who answered both principle questions AND all four calculations correctly

quantities.name: share_correct_on_average_and_total_comprehension
quantities.baseline: Study 3b: both principle-check questions and all four calculation checks correct

our_assessment.why: Reproduces. The averagist preference in 3b is not a comprehension artifact: it is at least as strong among the 5.6% who demonstrably understood that totals were equal (2.18 vs 2.31). The quantitative content worth carrying for longtermist arguments: for HAPPY populations, multiplying the population by 10,000 recovers about a quarter of what a 20-point drop in average costs, and beyond a million people each further factor of ten moves the answer by ~0.02 scale points -- lay value of happy numbers is saturated. For unhappy populations the same multiplication recovers more than the whole loss; that valence contrast carries the same reverse-coding confound as c4 and should not be cited as a welfare asymmetry. 3d gender test: the printed t(571) and means are those of the UNEXCLUDED sample (N=613), not the reported N=482 (reanalysis/s3bd.py); same conclusion either way.

relations.why: Independent lab (economics, reasons framing) finds the absolute Asymmetry a minority view too (12-15%); but there the Asymmetry outnumbers its mirror 57:17, here 12:10 -- see spears2020#c3.
Same lay axiology from a different design: future numbers barely enter unprompted judgments; describing the future as good moves them strongly (utopia condition 67-77% vs control 19-24%).

Both treat an elicited number (a trade ratio here, an extinction probability there) as a measurement of a format-independent quantity behind the elicitation. Karger's own data show the format moves the number by up to 800,000x; this paper reports in passing that 'in additional preliminary studies the trade ratio can also heavily depend on the framing of the question' and does not report those studies. Both literatures feed longtermist priority arguments with numbers whose format-dependence is acknowledged and unmeasured.

Same lesson from a different construct: the centre of a distribution of judgments (here the mean trade ratio, there the conditional mean of well-being) is reported as the finding while the shape -- a 37% cluster at exact symmetry, a heavy tail of ratios -- carries the substantive content.

Per the EA Forum summary (forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/poZwKfPPtgCmTQcBk), Evaluator 2 questioned the neutral-person result (M=4.23, d=0.35) -- which c3 here finds half-carried by wrong-sign responders -- and neither evaluator raised the reverse-coding / post-treatment-baseline issue of c4 or the scale-dependence of c2. That summary is secondary; verify against the reports before citing it.

Does a separately randomised neutral arm (not asked after the valenced items) show the size aversion that World S in reanalysis/s3a_identifiability.py predicts (4.08, 3.44, 3.02 at 1k/1M/1B)? That one arm decides c4.

The paper's 'preliminary studies' in which the trade ratio 'heavily depends on the framing' and in which a deontic (button-press) framing gave higher ratios are not in the OSF deposit. Their size is the size of the format effect on the paper's headline number.

Study 3c's 26% comprehension exclusion (96 participants read level 0 as 'extremely unhappy'): is the -100..+100 scale read by many as 0..100? If so, Studies 1b, 3b-3d inherit a scale-reading problem only 3c tested for.
Bruers (Unjournal E1) proposed reversing the 1a question ('...for this world to be overall NEGATIVE'). If the threshold moves, c1's 1.5-3x is partly an anchoring effect of the question's direction.
